blocks.text: Mariana Cook – Photographing time, inhabiting elsewhere

There are photographers whose gaze does more than simply capture the world; it seeks to reveal its most elusive dimensions. Mariana Cook belongs to that rare category of artists for whom photography is as much an inward experience as it is an act of creation. From her earliest portraits onwards, she has developed a profoundly humanistic body of work, attentive to the singularity of individuals, to their presence as well as to what remains beyond our grasp. Her approach, at once intuitive and exacting, never seeks to impose an interpretation. Instead, she allows a certain emotional truth to emerge from the silence of the image. Renowned for her extraordinarily compelling portraits of figures from the worlds of art, literature and politics, Mariana Cook has never regarded photography as a mere exercise in representation. What interests her is less the identity of her subjects than what they reveal, sometimes unknowingly. Her gaze, free from any desire for theatrical staging, favours presence, the intensity of a fleeting moment and the complexity of an individual personality. It is a way of looking that reflects a profound attentiveness to the world and to its many forms of existence. With her latest project, she makes a shift that is as unexpected as it is deeply coherent: having photographed human faces, she now turns her attention to stones. Yet this passage from the human to the mineral world is in no way a departure. Rather, it extends, in another form, the same quest for presence and identity.
In Basel, an intimate geography of exile and memory

Presented at the Kulturstiftung Basel H. Geiger, the exhibition brings together the results of eleven years of travel, research and encounters around the world. Mariana Cook explores the world of glacial erratics: monumental boulders torn from their original landscapes and carried by glaciers, sometimes over vast distances, before being deposited in unfamiliar surroundings. Silent witnesses to geological upheavals spanning millennia, these stones carry within them a history of displacement, rupture and transformation. Through the photographer’s lens, they cease to be mere geological curiosities and become subjects in their own right. Some seem to possess an almost human presence; others assert their solitude against the vastness of the landscape. Through the richness of its tonal range and the precision of its contrasts, black and white reveals their texture, volume and sculptural power, while lending them an almost timeless quality. The source of this fascination lies in a deeply personal identification. Mariana Cook acknowledges seeing herself in these displaced stones, estranged from their surroundings and destined to exist elsewhere. Through them, she subtly evokes a sense of uprootedness and otherness that reaches far beyond her own experience. The exhibition thus becomes a meditation on exile, belonging, solitude and the possibility of finding one’s place in a world that is not necessarily the one from which one comes. Curated by Beda Achermann, who also conceived the book accompanying the project, and complemented by a documentary film by Evelyn Schels, the exhibition unfolds as a deeply engaging visual and emotional experience. It invites visitors to slow down, to look differently, and to contemplate the depth of time that precedes us and ultimately transcends us. For behind these mineral landscapes lies a more universal reflection on the human condition: that of beings in motion, shaped by memory, sometimes strangers to themselves, and forever in search of a place to belong. With this body of work, so deeply coherent in its poetic vision, Mariana Cook reminds us that photography is not merely about fixing what is visible, but also about making perceptible what remains buried beneath the surface. Her stones possess the presence of human beings, and their silence seems to hold stories waiting to be told. In photographing them, she does more than document the traces of an ancient world: she gives form to a profoundly contemporary emotion — that of elsewhere, and of what it means to belong in the world.

A photographic memory from your childhood? My father used to take slides and let me look through a plastic stereoscopic viewer. A luminous world opened before my eyes.
The camera of your childhood? First a “Brownie.” Then a Kodak Instamatic.
The one you use today? Hasselblad and Rolleiflex.
The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Alfred Stieglitz.
The image you wish you had taken? Thankfully, I can’t remember.

And which photograph changed your world? The portrait I made of Barack and Michelle Obama in 1996 was first seen by the public in 2009, when it was published simultaneously in Le Monde and The New Yorker . It is celebrated because I photographed them for my “Couples” project before he went into politics. But most importantly to me, it is a successful portrait in terms of both its emotional content and its complex yet seemingly simple composition.
A key image in your personal pantheon? The self-portrait I made in 1981, “Self-Portrait on Wheels.”

Elliott Erwitt said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretative.” Do you agree? Black and white is interpretive, by definition, because it is an abstraction from what most people think of as real – a world full of descriptive color.

In your opinion, can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Sometimes technique itself can elicit an emotional response. On the other hand, the “emotion” in a picture may touch one viewer and leave another cold.
What elements can make silence visible in a photograph? Tonal range.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Can a photograph be truer than reality? If an image is original in some way, its uniqueness could come from a moment, from staging, from reality or not.
Can a photograph change our perception of an event? Of course.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? It could be one or both, depending on who is looking at the picture and their respective perceptions of the subject, independent of the image itself. It is also possible that our understanding of a picture may change, or that it may affect us differently as we age and perceive life differently.
In your opinion, what quality is necessary to be a good photographer? Not being the center of attention.
How do you choose your projects? Something grabs hold of me, and I can’t shake it until I make the pictures.
How would you describe your creative process? Intuitive.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? My pictures of glacial erratics. I identify with these displaced rocks, carried by ice sheets for millennia before being dropped on alien land, forever destined to be outsiders, as I often feel myself to be. I spent eleven years traveling the world on a kind of treasure hunt for these stones. The exhibition and accompanying book, curated and designed by Beda Achermann, along with a documentary film by Evelyn Schels, will be on view at the Kulturstiftung Basel H. Geiger Foundation in Basel from November 20 to February 14.
The person you would like to photograph? I would like to photograph Beda Achermann, who has curated my exhibition in Basel and designed an original and beautiful book to accompany it.
The person by whom you would like to be photographed? I am considering making another self-portrait.
An essential photography book? John Szarkowski’s Looking at Photographs is very good. America and Alfred Stieglitz meant a lot to me, as did Camera Notes and Camera Work .
What is the last photograph you took? I made portraits of the writers Garth Greenwell and Luis Muñoz, together and individually. I haven’t printed them yet.
What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? People are more practiced at looking at photographs.

What is your view on AI? AI is a tool that can be applied to benefit human beings in many ways. To the extent that it is used to make pictures, it will soon surpass the capabilities of human practitioners who embrace “appropriation” as both a methodology and a source of content.
Color or black and white? I don’t see in color.
Natural light or artificial light? Natural light only, please.
Which city seems the most photogenic to you? New York City.
A place you never tire of? New York City.
The image that, for you, represents the current state of the world? There is no “current state” of the whole world, and certainly no photograph that can represent it in its entirety.
In your opinion, what is missing in today’s world? Tactility.
Your favorite drug? Advil.
Your best way to disconnect? Sleep.
Your greatest professional extravagance? Photographic paper.
If you had to start all over again? I would do the same thing.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be at the table? I always enjoy meeting people I have never met before who make the most original contributions in their respective fields and are humble.
What do you like people to say about you… after you’re gone? I wonder if Mariana would be surprised to know how much more her pictures have been appreciated since her death.
